The Ni-based superalloy was manufactured via a powder metallurgy process including hot isostatic pressing and hot extrusion.
The chemical composition of the Ni-based superalloy is provided in Table 1.
The isothermal hot compression experiments were conducted using a Gleeble 3500-GTC thermal-mechanical testing system.
The total true strain applied during the hot compression experiments was -0.69.
The microstructure examination revealed the presence of fabrication-induced voids and pores in the as-received powder metallurgy superalloy.
The true stress-strain curves exhibited characteristics of dynamic recrystallization and dynamic strain aging.
The peak stress and peak strain increased at lower temperatures and higher strain rates.
The finite element analysis showed that the maximum tensile stress was located at the outer bulging surfaces of the samples, causing failure initiation.
The critical failure strain, ε_f, was extracted from the FEA simulation and also determined based on the evolution of void volume fraction.
The failure strain remained nearly insensitive to the range of strain rates considered, while it increased with the increase of temperature in a third-order polynomial relationship.
The processing maps with failure domains were constructed by combining the power dissipation map, flow instability map, and the failure map derived from the FEA simulations.
The Gurson-Tvergaard-Needleman (GTN) damage model was employed in the finite element analysis to predict the failure threshold of the powder metallurgy superalloy.
The variation of friction coefficients between 0.3 and 1.0 did not significantly affect the stress contours of the samples during hot compression.
Temperature was found to be a more controlling factor than strain rate in the failure behaviors of the powder metallurgy Ni-based superalloy.
Lower temperatures and higher strain rates resulted in more severe tensile stress and earlier failure in the samples.
